bullets: **Part (a)**: an extract is printed. You explore how Dickens presents a character, theme or idea **in the extract**. 20 marks, **AO2** (language, form, structure).

**Part (b)**: you explain the importance of the same theme or character **elsewhere in the novella**. 20 marks, **AO1** (response, argument, references) and **AO3** (context). You must refer to context.
Suggested time: roughly 25–30 minutes on each part (around 55–60 minutes total). Follow your school’s advice for the whole paper.
core.p: Paper 2 Section A: one question on your 19th-century novel, in two parts. Check the marks and AOs printed on your paper.

bullets: Read the question, underline the focus.
Read the extract twice; annotate 5–6 moments: key words, imagery, sentence structure, narrative voice, dialogue, shifts.
Find the **shape**: how does the extract begin, turn and end?
Write 3–4 paragraphs following the extract’s order: **point → short quotation → zoom on a word or technique → effect on the reader → why Dickens does this**.
No context needed in (a) (it is AO2); focus on methods.
Write a **thesis** linking the theme to Dickens’s purpose.
Choose 3–4 moments from **different staves** (not the extract).
Each paragraph: point → reference/quotation → explanation → **context** woven in → link to Dickens’s purpose.
Track **change** across the novella: Stave 1 → Stave 5 is the most powerful frame.

callouts.p: Context must explain why Dickens wrote something: Poor Law, Malthus, child labour, Ragged Schools, Christmas revival, Dickens’s childhood.

core.h: Model part (a) opening paragraph (Stave 1 description of Scrooge)
core.p: Dickens introduces Scrooge through an explosive list of participles: he is a ‘squeezing, wrenching, grasping, scraping, clutching, covetous, old sinner!’. The asyndetic list piles up verbs of physical grasping, as though Scrooge clings to money with his whole body, and the final noun ‘sinner’ adds a religious judgement. The simile ‘solitary as an oyster’ suggests he is closed off and hard on the outside, yet an oyster can hold a pearl, hinting at the goodness that the ghosts will later uncover.

model: Cold imagery: ‘The cold within him froze his old features’
exam.q: Part (a): Explore how Dickens presents Scrooge in this extract (Stave 1, the opening description). (20 marks)
exam.tip: Pick the 5–6 richest words and say what each one does.

mistakes.r: Part (b) must use other parts of the novella.
mistakes.w: Using the extract again in part (b).

mistakes.r: Part (a) rewards AO2; context there earns little.
Every paragraph needs an argument and a purpose.

summary: The A Christmas Carol question has two parts: (a) an extract analysis worth 20 marks for AO2, and (b) a whole-text response on the same theme or character worth 20 marks for AO1 and AO3; this note gives the method, timing and paragraph structure for both.

terms.d: Language, form and structure: the whole of part (a).
An informed, personal response with references: part (b).
